title: Leading Change in Industrialization 4.0/5.0 (Chapter 13, Humanity Amplified)
author: Stefan Bauschard
summary: In Chapter 13 of his Industrialization 4.0/5.0 series, Stefan Bauschard argues that AI is changing what schools are for: the institutions that long held a society's knowledge are seeing that role slip even as they retain the expertise needed to navigate the transition. Educators therefore face two simultaneous jobs — building AI into how they teach and preparing students for an AI-entangled future — inside institutions known for resisting change. Drawing on classic leadership theory (Burns on transformational leadership, Drucker on opportunity over problems, Kotter on the leadership/management distinction, Bennis on turning vision into reality, Sandberg on authenticity), he insists change must begin with people and with the institution's mission and values rather than with tools, and proposes a 'Head of AI' role to convert intention into practice. He also makes a candid, evidence-weighted case for diverse leadership — conceding that the often-cited McKinsey claim that diversity boosts financial performance failed independent replication, while arguing the firmer ground is judgment: diverse teams are better placed to catch AI's absorbed biases, as MIT Media Lab facial-recognition findings illustrate.
points: AI is shifting what schools are for: their historic role as the home of a society's knowledge is slipping even as they still hold much of the expertise needed for the transition.
Educators face two jobs at once — building AI into how they teach and preparing students for an AI-entangled future — inside institutions long known for resisting change.
Leading the shift should start with people and with the institution's mission, values and goals rather than with tools; a dedicated 'Head of AI' role turns strategy into working practice.
The case for diverse leadership rests on judgment, not the balance sheet: Bauschard concedes the popular McKinsey financial-performance claim failed independent replication.
Diverse teams are better placed to catch the biases AI absorbs from human data — as MIT Media Lab findings on facial recognition misjudging darker-skinned and female faces show.
quotes: For centuries, a society’s schools and universities were where its knowledge lived and where people went to acquire it.
Educators therefore face two jobs at once: to build AI into how they teach, and to prepare students for a future thoroughly entangled with it.
Peter Drucker built his idea of leadership around opportunity rather than problems, asking not “what is broken?” but “what is now possible that wasn’t before?
Leadership sets the direction; management makes the thing run.
The firmer ground for diverse leadership is not the balance sheet but judgment.
AI systems learn from enormous bodies of human data, and they absorb the biases sitting in that data along the way
